solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Quaffed, according to Connery, in cheap joint?

indicators.note: Sean Connery famously says an S as SH, so this phrase asks for a word as his accent would render it

parts.note: to quaff is to drink deeply, so quaffed means sank, as in sank a pint

explanation.surface: A question about what Sean Connery downed in some cheap dive bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'joint' reads as a cheap bar, but it is a cut of meat; Connery's slushy S turns SANK into SHANK.
explanation.definitionFit: The shank is the lower leg, one of the cheaper cuts a butcher sells for slow cooking.

clue.text: Swell to drop by on sucker in the US

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on another sits above it, so the first piece comes first

parts.note: to drop by is to pop in, call briefly
jay is American slang for a gullible, easily fooled person

explanation.surface: Instructions to go and see an American mark and get puffed up about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell' looks like a verb but is the old noun for a dandy.
explanation.definitionFit: A swell is a showy dandy, and a popinjay is likewise a vain, foppishly dressed person.

clue.text: Poet's song of praise unfinished in scripture reading?

definitions.note: the definition is the poet; the 's stands for is, joining it to the wordplay

indicators.note: the shortened hymn sits in the middle of the scripture lesson

parts.note: RE is religious education, the school scripture lesson

indicators.note: the last letter of the song word is lopped off, so it is not finished

parts.note: a hymn is a song praising God
reading is one of the three Rs, so it gives R

explanation.surface: A poet's hymn left incomplete during a Bible reading in church.
explanation.walkthrough: RE is religious education, the British school subject, and reading gives R as one of the three Rs; 'unfinished' trims the song and 'in' sets it within RE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who writes rhyming verse is a versifier, a humble kind of poet.

clue.text: Fashionable crowd avoiding Spain this month

parts.note: something fashionable is in

indicators.note: the trendy group keeps clear of Spain, so its letter leaves the word

parts.note: a set is a crowd or clique
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: The trendy crowd is giving Spain a miss for their holidays this month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'avoiding' removes the E from INSET.
explanation.definitionFit: Inst., short for instant, is old business-letter shorthand for the current calendar month.

clue.text: With which to augment — when ground — a light cappuccino?

definitions.text: With which to augment — when ground — a light cappuccino?

indicators.note: grinding breaks the word up, so the letters of augment are rearranged
light here means lacking, so the A is what the jumbled word sheds

explanation.surface: A query about what spice to grate over a frothy coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when ground' scrambles AUGMENT and 'a light' drops its A, leaving the letters of the spice; the whole clue also describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: The ground seed of this tree is a spice often dusted on top of milky coffees.

clue.text: A kid's gone off the rails, as Hogarth saw the mother?

indicators.note: a child gone off the rails has gone wrong, so these letters go astray into a new order

explanation.surface: A youngster has gone astray, much as Hogarth pictured the boozy mother in his print.
explanation.walkthrough: Hogarth's engraving Gin Lane shows a drunken mother letting her baby fall.
explanation.definitionFit: Hogarth depicted the mother in Gin Lane as sodden with spirits, utterly drunk on cheap liquor.

clue.text: High snow drifts engulfing Oscar, going like the wind!

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step
snow that drifts is blown about, so these letters are shifted into a new order

parts.note: Oscar is the NATO alphabet code word for O

explanation.surface: A blizzard scene: deep snow piling up and swallowing someone called Oscar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drifts' scrambles HIGH SNOW, and 'engulfing' puts O among those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving with a rushing sound at great speed is going like the wind.

clue.text: Capital city regularly excusing truancies

indicators.note: letting off every other letter, so only the alternate ones remain

explanation.surface: A city authority routinely forgiving pupils who skip school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly excusing' keeps the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters of truancies.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the seat of government of Tunisia in North Africa.

clue.text: Hired gun in metal band?

parts.note: a gun is a firearm, an arm
to let property is to hire it out, so let means hired

explanation.surface: A mercenary gunman playing in a heavy metal group.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in the opposite order to the clue: the gun first, then the past participle meaning hired out.
explanation.definitionFit: A bracelet worn round the upper arm, often of metal, is a band for that limb.

clue.text: Shaky batting, getting 13

parts.note: a cricketer who is batting is in
13 is the answer to 13 Down, rigid, and firm means rigid

explanation.surface: A cricket report: a nervous batsman stiffening up at the crease.
explanation.walkthrough: The 13 points to the answer of 13 Down, whose synonym supplies the second part.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone infirm is frail and unsteady on their feet.

clue.text: Sweet thing from Mauritius mixed with upper-class once

indicators.note: the island's name is mixed up, so its letters are rearranged
the posh letter appears only once, so one of the two copies in the island's name is surplus

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for upper-class, as in U and non-U

explanation.surface: A dessert from Mauritius blended with posh ingredients in days gone by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed' scrambles MAURITIUS; 'with upper-class once' says the U appears once, so one U goes.
explanation.definitionFit: This Italian coffee-and-mascarpone pudding is a sweet, the British word for dessert.

clue.text: Juliet Harrison's touring coastal features

indicators.note: the Fords go round the letter as if on tour around it

parts.note: the actor Harrison Ford, with the possessive s making the plural
Juliet is the NATO alphabet code word for J

explanation.surface: Someone called Juliet travelling with the Harrison family along a coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'touring' puts J inside FORDS, from Harrison Ford's surname plus the S of the possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Long narrow sea inlets between steep cliffs, as in Norway, shape a coastline.

clue.text: Mother buried dog's body

indicators.note: mother is buried, put out of sight, so her letters vanish from the breed

parts.note: a mastiff is a large breed of dog
ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: A grieving mother laid her pet dog's remains in the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'buried' removes MA from MASTIFF.
explanation.definitionFit: Stiff is slang for a corpse, a dead body.

clue.text: Block record first episodes of Just a Minute

parts.note: a log is a written record, as in a ship's log

indicators.note: the opening of each word of the show's title, like a show's first episodes

explanation.surface: Someone recording the early episodes of the BBC radio panel game Just a Minute.
explanation.walkthrough: Just a Minute is a long-running BBC radio panel show.
explanation.definitionFit: A jam of floating timber blocking a river gives the word for any blockage.

clue.text: I moan & moan furiously — it's an obsession

indicators.note: moaning furiously suggests a wild jumble, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A grumbler complaining over and over in a rage about a fixation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'furiously' scrambles I MOAN MOAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixation on a single idea or subject is an obsession.

clue.text: Inquisitive lad returning last thing on Friday

indicators.note: coming back means the word for the boy is read backwards

parts.note: a son is a lad, a boy

indicators.note: the final letter of the weekday is taken

explanation.surface: A curious boy coming home late at the end of the week.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' reads the boy backwards, and 'last thing on Friday' looks like a time of day but just takes the weekday's final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosy person pokes into others' business, being prying and curious.

clue.text: Indicate player in an off-side position

definitions.meaning: in cricket, ... is a fielder on the off side square of the batsman

explanation.surface: A football referee signalling that a player has strayed offside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off-side' suggests football's offside rule, but it is cricket: the off side is the half of the field the batsman faces, and point is a fielding position there.
explanation.definitionFit: Pointing directs attention, and the cricket fielder takes the name of the fielding spot.

clue.text: Photographs capturing whistle-blower given title

indicators.note: the photos catch and hold the official within them

parts.note: pix is informal for pictures or photographs
a referee, ref, blows the whistle in football

explanation.surface: Pictures of a whistle-blower given a fancy title in the press.
explanation.walkthrough: 'whistle-blower' suggests an informant; here it is the referee.
explanation.definitionFit: A title such as Dr or Sir placed before a name is a prefix to it.

clue.text: Stop knocking back meths, having dumped husband

indicators.note: the husband is thrown out, so his letter leaves
drinking the spirit, knocking it back, read here as turning the word backwards

explanation.surface: A plea to stop someone drinking methylated spirits after leaving her husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocking back' reverses METHS to SHTEM, and 'having dumped husband' takes out the H.
explanation.definitionFit: To stem a flow of blood or water is to stop it.

clue.text: Small space stocking beer, where lots get hammered

indicators.note: the small space stocks the drink, holding it within

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
room means space, as in room to move
ale is a type of beer

explanation.surface: A tiny room crammed with beer, where crowds get drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hammered' suggests drunk drinkers, but lots here are auction items knocked down by the auctioneer's hammer.
explanation.definitionFit: Auction lots are sold under the hammer in a saleroom.

clue.text: One getting into the groove down on the floor?

definitions.text: One getting into the groove down on the floor?

parts.words: One getting into the groove down on the floor?
parts.note: floorboards are jointed by a projecting ridge on one board that slots into a channel cut in the next

explanation.surface: A dancer finding the rhythm on the dance floor.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is disco dancing; the clue really describes the joint used in floorboards.
explanation.definitionFit: The projecting edge of a board that fits a matching channel is named after the mouth's muscular organ.

clue.text: Tucking into Darjeeling (a tea), upside-down cake

indicators.note: the cake is tucked into the run of words, sitting inside them

explanation.surface: Someone eating an upside-down cake with a cup of Darjeeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upside-down' seems to say reverse, but it is only part of the text in which the cake is found, in Darjeelin(g a tea u)pside.
explanation.definitionFit: This French word for a rich, cream-filled sponge is used in English for a fancy cake.

clue.text: Weak, backsliding constituent of Iron Lady?

indicators.note: the reversed word becomes a part of the iron symbol, placed inside it

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

indicators.note: sliding back means the word for weak is read backwards

parts.note: a lame excuse is a weak one

explanation.surface: A jibe at Margaret Thatcher, the Iron Lady, as a feeble, backsliding member of her party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron Lady' looks like one phrase, Margaret Thatcher's nickname, but Lady alone is the definition; 'backsliding' reverses the word for weak and 'constituent of' sets it inside the iron symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: A lady is a woman, and woman as an adjective is the sex opposite to male.

clue.text: Brussels to support 50% reduction of defence element

indicators.note: in a down clue, a supporting piece goes beneath, so this piece comes last
halving the word, so only the first four of its eight letters remain

parts.note: a nation's defence is its military
Brussels is home to the European Union's institutions, so it stands for EU

explanation.surface: The EU propping up a nation whose defence budget has been cut in half.
explanation.walkthrough: '50% reduction of' halves MILITARY to MILI, and 'to support' puts EU below it.
explanation.definitionFit: A milieu is someone's surroundings, the setting in which they are in their element.

clue.text: Find shelter in 5th Avenue

indicators.note: the shelter sits inside the street name, spanning its two words

explanation.surface: Someone seeking refuge somewhere on New York's Fifth Avenue.
explanation.walkthrough: The word sits across the two words: 5t(h Aven)ue.
explanation.definitionFit: A haven is a place of safety or refuge.

clue.text: Part of Manhattan — you should eventually see summer here

definitions.meaning: the district of New York City lying between Fifth Avenue and the East River

definitions.text: you should eventually see summer here
definitions.meaning: the grid hides a message, and SUMMER is spelt out down the right-hand edge of the grid

explanation.surface: A tip that summer reaches a certain part of Manhattan in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half points to the puzzle's hidden message: the seasons are spelt round the edges of the grid, and summer is on the right-hand side.
explanation.definitionFit: The right-hand side of a map faces the rising sun, so it is that compass point's flank.

clue.text: Leave former partner over sexual relations

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece over another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: an ex is a former spouse or partner
it is a coy word for sex

explanation.surface: Advice to walk out on an ex after a row about sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' puts EX above IT in the down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To exit a room is to leave it.

clue.text: Immature youngsters left adult rave drunk

parts.note: A was the film rating for adult films

indicators.note: a drunk party wobbles, so these letters lurch into a new order

explanation.surface: Teenagers abandoned at a grown-up all-night party, now drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' scrambles RAVE to RVAE.
explanation.definitionFit: Grubs and caterpillars are the immature young of insects.

clue.text: Drive ball, knocking the covers off in match

indicators.note: stripping the outer letters, the covers, from each word

explanation.surface: A cricket batsman hitting the ball hard during a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocking the covers off' strips D and E from Drive and B and L from ball, leaving RIV and AL. 'covers' also hints at the cricket fielding position.
explanation.definitionFit: To rival someone is to equal or match them.

clue.text: Military might sack captured soldier (engineer, rtd)

parts.note: to sack someone is to fire them
POW stands for prisoner of war

indicators.note: rtd, short for retired, here means turned back, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army's engineering corps

explanation.surface: A military bulletin: a soldier captured and dismissed, plus a retired engineer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rtd' (retired) reverses RE, the Royal Engineers, to ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Firepower is the destructive capacity of an army's guns, its military strength.
